If I want to not give support to a site, but I end up clicking on a link and getting my IP address logged, is there a sort of "in for a penny, in for a pound" logic that might as well take over? I don't see websites reporting their statistics in unique visitors per day; I tend to see it more as "Website X had 100 million unique visitors per month."

I think it would make more sense to advertisers if they demanded total pageview stats from sites, and also total number of seconds spent with the page up, so that a person who accidentally clicks on a link and then immediately closes the window isn't registering the same as a person who spends five hours a day clicking on hundreds of pages and threads.
If websites sell their ad space based on "unique visitors per month," is there any point in boycotting a site if you end up clicking on a link to it by mistake once per month?

Suppose there are 30 days in a month, and let's round up to 102 million unique visitors for easier division. Then per day there's on average 3.4 million unique visitors. The reason why they wouldn't do it per day is that some days they might drop to 1 million whereas other days they might spike to 8 million.

If they average 100 million a day it would make them seem a lot more consistent, which would draw more advertisers to the website. In fact I think they would log the unique visitors per day, but then just sum the last 30 days rather than distinguishing if there are any duplicates to increase the number. The accidental clicks are also likely logged to increase the numbers to appeal to more advertisers. This is marketing to advertisers and sponsors, not metrics for them.

I'd like to touch on something I don't see mentioned yet. In regards to offensive content, Reddit and Voat have two different approaches. Reddit plays content police and decides what offensive content to ban site wide. If you think Reddit's content policy goes too far (or not far enough) you're out of luck. Voat instead puts those tools in users' hands. If you find a subverse offensive, you yourself can block it and never see it again. Be as petty as you like with your content policy because it's your content policy, and it doesn't directly affect anyone but you. Of the two systems, I think that Voat's provides more flexibility and doesn't silence others unnecessarily just because there's something I don't want to see. On the other side of the coin I have the power to block content that may not be covered by a site wide policy. It wins out both ways.
